title: AARP sees a goldmine hiding in plain sight in AI adoption

content_html:
Damilola Esebame

Mon, August 3, 2026 at 10:07 AM EDT 4 min read

Artificial intelligence (AI) investment is becoming common across workplaces, and decisions about how those tools are deployed are often being made by leaders over 40.

That finding, from a recent AARP employer survey, is one that the organization argues should change how companies approach workforce AI training.

Yet the same employees steering those decisions are largely shut out of formal training programs built to sharpen fluency with the technology they oversee.

A new analysis from AARP's Public Policy Institute, drawing on Urban Institute research, argues that companies are sidelining their most valuable AI asset: experienced workers.

Older workers drive AI decisions but rarely receive formal training

About 46% of employers say workers 40 and older make most or all decisions about how AI is used, AARP's Employers and AI study found.

That strategic influence has not translated into access to training, because only 12% of workers aged 50 and older have completed any AI-focused training or coursework.

About 49% of workers in that age group express interest in learning more about using AI at work, AARP's tracking survey on workforce trends confirmed.

The gap between interest and participation has narrowed only modestly across three survey waves, from 41 percentage points to 37, with demand near 49% and completion climbing only from 7% to 12%.

LinkedIn data reinforces the case that older professionals are not the reluctant technology learners many hiring managers assume them to be. Workers 50 and older who listed AI among their LinkedIn skills grew by 25% over five years, a joint AARP and LinkedIn report found.

That growth rate was nearly double what younger peers achieved during the same period, undercutting stereotypes about technology adoption after 50.

The durable skills employers say AI cannot replicate alone

A 2026 Urban Institute study concluded that companies need workers with durable, transferable skills to capture the productivity benefits AI promises.

The research, based on interviews with business leaders, AI experts, and workplace education providers, identified creative problem-solving, critical thinking, ethical oversight, and judgment as capabilities employers need most.

  • Microsoft CEO sends a blunt warning on AI and the tech ecosystem

These skills, shaped by decades of professional experience, are held by older workers and influence every AI-related decision their companies ask them to make.

content_html_zh:
达米洛拉·埃塞巴梅

2026 年 8 月 3 日星期一，美国东部时间上午 10:07 阅读 4 分钟

人工智能 (AI) 投资在工作场所变得越来越普遍，有关如何部署这些工具的决策通常由 40 岁以上的领导者做出。

美国退休人员协会 (AARP) 最近的一项雇主调查得出的这一发现，该组织认为应该改变公司进行劳动力人工智能培训的方式。

然而，指导这些决策的员工在很大程度上被排除在旨在提高他们所监督的技术熟练程度的正式培训计划之外。

美国退休人员协会公共政策研究所根据城市研究所的研究进行的一项新分析认为，公司正在放弃其最有价值的人工智能资产：经验丰富的员工。

年长员工推动人工智能决策，但很少接受正式培训

AARP 的雇主与人工智能研究发现，约 46% 的雇主表示，40 岁及以上的员工对如何使用人工智能做出了大部分或全部决定。

这种战略影响并没有转化为获得培训的机会，因为在 50 岁及以上的员工中，只有 12% 完成了任何以人工智能为重点的培训或课程。

AARP 对劳动力趋势的跟踪调查证实，该年龄段的员工中约有 49% 表示有兴趣了解更多有关在工作中使用人工智能的信息。

在三轮调查中，兴趣和参与度之间的差距仅小幅缩小，从 41 个百分点缩小到 37 个百分点，需求接近 49%，而完成率仅从 7% 攀升至 12%。

LinkedIn 的数据进一步证明，老年专业人士并不像许多招聘经理所认为的那样不情愿地学习技术。 美国退休人员协会 (AARP) 和 LinkedIn 的联合报告发现，5 岁及以上将人工智能列为 LinkedIn 技能的员工在五年内增长了 25%。

这一增长率几乎是同期年轻同龄人的两倍，打破了人们对 50 岁以后采用技术的刻板印象。

雇主称人工智能无法单独复制持久技能

城市研究所 2026 年的一项研究得出的结论是，公司需要具有持久、可转移技能的工人来获得人工智能所承诺的生产力优势。

该研究基于对商界领袖、人工智能专家和职场教育提供者的采访，确定创造性解决问题、批判性思维、道德监督和判断力是雇主最需要的能力。

更多人工智能：

  • 高盛向人工智能股票投资者发出直言不讳的信息
  • 微软首席执行官对人工智能和科技生态系统发出直言不讳的警告
  • 下一场人工智能基础设施竞赛与芯片无关

这些技能由数十年的专业经验形成，由年长的员工掌握，并影响公司要求他们做出的每一个与人工智能相关的决策。
